"You stopped coming to the Sunday youth group," Thomas said, dropping his bag on Kunal's bed.
"I didn't stop. I'm taking a break."
"From God or from us?"
Kunal laughed, then his smile slipped. "From being told what to think before I've thought it. I've been reading. Some of it makes sense, some of it scares me."
"Like what?"
"Like whether I believe the things I say in prayers, or I just know the words."
Thomas sat down. "My dad would say doubt is part of faith."
"Would you say it?"
"I don't know. I've never asked myself." Thomas picked at the bedsheet. "Can I read what you're reading?"
"Only if you argue with me properly. No quoting your dad."
"Deal. But you come back one Sunday and argue there too."
Kunal thought about it. "One Sunday. Then I decide."

qa.q: Why did Kunal say he was taking a break from the youth group?
qa.a: He said he was taking a break from being told what to think before he had thought it.

qa.q: What might Kunal be feeling about his reading, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He feels curious but also a little scared; he says some of it makes sense and some of it scares him, and his laugh fades when Thomas asks.

qa.q: How could Thomas support Kunal while he works out what he believes?
qa.a: He can keep reading and arguing with Kunal honestly, without pressure, and leave the final decision to him.

qa.q: How is Thomas affected by Kunal's questions?
qa.a: Kunal's questions make Thomas notice he has never asked himself what he believes, so he wants to read the same books.

grounding: Shows a teenager questioning inherited religious belief and testing ideas before choosing a position.

Last winter my cousin Sarita dragged me to a meeting about the lake behind our colony. People were dumping construction rubble in it, and the old men there spoke like it was a war. I went for the samosas. I stayed because a woman showed a photo of the lake from when my Appa was a boy, full of birds.
After that I read everything. For two months I was angry at every lorry. I posted long rants and argued at dinner until Appa left the table.
Then I noticed I was only repeating the loudest people. So I made myself read what the builders said too. I still believe the lake matters. But now I, Jomon, can say why, in my own words, and I listen before I shout.

qa.q: What did Jomon see in the photo at the meeting?
qa.a: A photo of the lake from when Appa was a boy, full of birds.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel in the two months after the meeting?
qa.a: Jomon felt angry at every lorry and fired up, posting rants and arguing at dinner.

qa.q: What would you advise a teen who has just found a cause they care about?
qa.a: Read the other side too, like Jomon did, so the belief is really their own and they can explain it calmly.

qa.q: How might Appa have seen Jomon's first two months?
qa.a: Appa probably found the dinner arguments tiring, which is why he left the table, though he may have been glad Jomon cared about the lake he knew as a boy.

grounding: Illustrates a teen moving from borrowed passion to a considered, personally owned civic belief.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 11 debate club
Sarita asked to see me after Tuesday's debate on whether religion belongs in public life. She had argued the side she was given, well, but afterwards she said she felt like a hypocrite. At home her family keeps a daily prayer; lately she has been questioning parts of it and felt guilty even thinking this.
Baljeet, her debate partner, waited outside and told me she had been quiet for days.
I did not tell her what to believe. I said questioning is a normal part of growing up and she can take her time. We listed which parts of her faith still feel true to her and which ones she is unsure about.
Next step: I suggested she talk with one adult at home she trusts, and we meet again in two weeks.

qa.q: What was the topic of Tuesday's debate?
qa.a: Whether religion belongs in public life.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling after the debate?
qa.a: She felt like a hypocrite and guilty for questioning parts of her family's daily prayer.

qa.q: What small step did the counsellor suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: The counsellor suggested talking with one trusted adult at home, which could ease Sarita's guilt and let her sort out her beliefs without hiding them.

qa.q: How does Baljeet seem to see Sarita's state?
qa.a: Baljeet noticed she had been quiet for days and seemed concerned enough to wait outside the counsellor's room.

grounding: Shows a teen sorting through inherited religious practice while forming her own beliefs, supported by a counsellor.

passage:
You want to know how I picked electrical work? Honestly, Gopika, it picked me a bit. In Class 9 I told everyone I'd be a doctor, because that's what toppers say. Then biology practicals started and I felt nothing. Zero.
Meanwhile our building's inverter kept dying, and I was the one opening it up with the watchman, reading the manual, asking the repair uncle a hundred questions. I'd lose three hours and not notice.
So I made a list. What am I good at? Patient with wires, good with my hands, bad with blood. What jobs use that? Electrician, electrical engineer, solar installer.
My parents were worried at first. I'm still Charu, still stubborn. But now when I talk about my future, I sound like myself.

qa.q: What did Charu first tell everyone in Class 9?
qa.a: That Charu would be a doctor, because that's what toppers say.

qa.q: What does Charu losing three hours over the inverter suggest about Charu's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Charu felt absorbed and genuinely interested in a way biology never did.

qa.q: What could Charu do next to test the list of possible jobs?
qa.a: Charu could spend a day with a solar installer or electrician, or try a short course, to see how the real work feels.

qa.q: How might Charu's parents have seen Charu's change of plan?
qa.a: They were worried at first, perhaps because doctor sounded safer, but they may come round as they see how excited Charu is.

grounding: Shows a teen imagining careers and matching personal strengths to real jobs.

Farida here, from the flat opposite. I've watched Pankaj on his balcony all summer.
In May he was always on a laptop with a sketchbook beside it. His mother told mine he wanted to design games. Then in June he started sitting with his grandfather's old radio, taking it apart. He'd hold up tiny pieces and squint.
One evening I heard him on the phone: "Maybe I don't want to make games. Maybe I want to make the things games run on."
By July he had two columns taped to the window: GOOD AT and JOBS. I couldn't read it all, but I saw "soldering" and "patience" crossed out and rewritten.
I don't know what he's decided. He looks less stressed than in May, though, and he hums while he works.

qa.a: Two columns: GOOD AT and JOBS.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have been feeling when he said he wanted to make the things games run on?

qa.q: How could a parent support Pankaj's search?
qa.a: A parent could ask about his two columns and help him meet someone who builds electronics, without pushing either plan.

qa.q: How does Farida see Pankaj's summer?
qa.a: Farida sees his work change and notices he looks less stressed and hums, though she admits she doesn't know what he has decided.

Before: When Irawati cancelled their movie plan for the third time, Aparna typed a sharp message and deleted it. She sent "whatever 👍" instead and went quiet for a week. That was how her older cousins handled friends: cut them off before they cut you.
During: On Friday, Irawati's little brother mentioned their grandmother was in hospital. Aparna felt her stomach drop. Irawati hadn't said a word.
After: The next Monday Aparna walked over at lunch. "I'm sorry I went cold. I want to be the kind of friend who asks first." Irawati's eyes filled. "I didn't know how to say it."
That evening Aparna wrote in her notebook: ask before assuming. Show up. She decided that was the friend she meant to be.

passage:
Sit, Manjula. You asked why I still phone my brother every Sunday even though we fight.
When I was about fifteen, my brother and I shared one room and one cycle. I was mean to him. I hid the cycle key, I told Amma his secrets. I thought that was simply how older sisters behaved.
Then one night he had a high fever and Amma was on night shift. I sat with him, wiping his forehead, and he whispered, "Thank you, didi." Nobody had ever thanked me for being kind to him, because I never had been.
Next morning I gave him the key. I decided then: I would be a sister he could count on, even when he annoyed me.
So I, Sharmila, phone every Sunday. That is the sister I chose.

qa.q: What did Sharmila hide from her brother?
qa.a: She hid the cycle key.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have felt when her brother whispered thank you?
qa.a: She likely felt touched and ashamed at once, because nobody had thanked her for kindness she had never shown before.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Sharmila's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Sitting with her brother during his fever; it showed her what kind of sister she could be and led her to give him the key.

qa.q: How might the brother have felt when he got the key back the next morning?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and relieved, seeing his sister begin to treat him differently.

grounding: An elder recalls deciding, as a teen, what kind of sister she wanted to be.

Himani had forty minutes before the last bus and a promise to keep. Nilesh, her friend since Class 3, had asked her to come to his first stage play at the community hall. Her mother had also asked her to be home for her cousin's engagement dinner.
The rain started as she left school. Autos were full. She ran through puddles and reached the hall soaked, just as the curtain rose. She watched his first scene from the back, clapped hard, then slipped out to catch the bus.
She texted him: "Saw you. You were brilliant. Couldn't stay, family dinner, tell me everything tomorrow."
On the bus she thought about it. She didn't have to choose one person over another. She could be someone who shows up, even for part of it, and tells the truth about why.

qa.q: How much time did Himani have before the last bus?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Himani seem to feel on the bus afterwards?
qa.a: She felt settled and a bit relieved that she had kept both promises in part and been honest with Nilesh.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Going for the first scene and texting Nilesh the truth worked, because she showed up for her friend and still kept her family commitment.

qa.q: If you were Nilesh, what would you want from Himani's text?
qa.a: You would likely feel seen and happy that she came in the rain, and look forward to telling her everything tomorrow.

grounding: Shows a teen deciding what sort of friend and family member she wants to be under time pressure.

Lakshmi, beta, you say your school has groups that won't mix. Let me tell you about my college hostel in Pune, long ago.
There were the Marathi boys, the Bengali boys, the rich boys with scooters. I, Lalit, was from a small town and fit nowhere. For the first term I ate alone and pretended to read.

Layla noticed it on the first cold morning in Manchester: half her year wore the same puffer jacket, cream with a small silver tag. By lunch the girls in it were the ones everyone crowded around.

Yuki, who had been her lab partner all term, looked at it and said, "It suits you, I suppose. You seem different, though."
For two days the popular table waved Layla over. On the third, someone said the tag was already "so last month."
Walking home, Layla zipped the jacket up to her chin and thought about the babysitting hours. Then she texted Yuki: "Chips tomorrow? Normal me."

In the girls' hostel of a Nashik junior college, status came from the terrace. Whoever sat on the water tank at night, with a speaker playing, was somebody.
Kalyani wanted to be up there. She started using the same slang as the tank girls, laughed a beat too loud at their jokes, and lent her phone charger to anyone who asked.
Rekha, her roommate, watched this for weeks. One night she asked, "Do you even like their music?"
Kalyani hesitated. "Not really. But they matter here."
"You matter here," Rekha said, and went back to her book.
The next night the tank girls called her up. Kalyani went, sat for twenty minutes, and came back down early. She told Rekha the view was nice but her neck hurt from nodding.

qa.q: Where did status come from in the hostel?
qa.a: From the terrace, sitting on the water tank at night.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani laugh a beat too loud at the tank girls' jokes?
qa.a: She wanted their approval badly and felt anxious to fit in with the girls who seemed to matter.

qa.q: How did Rekha's question help, and what else could a friend do?
qa.a: It made Kalyani notice she did not even like the music; a friend can keep gently asking what she really enjoys.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt watching Kalyani change for weeks?
qa.a: Rekha may have felt a little sad and worried that her roommate was hiding herself to win status.

grounding: Shows a hostel teen copying a group's habits to raise her standing, and her roommate's view of it.

Dear Sarika,
You asked what happened with the school band. Here's the honest version.
When I heard the band got to skip assembly and everyone wanted to sit near them, I signed up for drums. I don't even like drums. I just liked the idea of walking into the hall with sticks in my back pocket.

Pema

"I'm not bunking tomorrow."

In the village school's science fair, Rashmi's water-filter model got the lowest mark in her group. The judge, a teacher from the block office, wrote: "Idea good. Testing weak. No data."
Rashmi's face went hot. Hemant, her partner, had built the frame and said loudly, "He doesn't understand village conditions."
Rashmi almost agreed. Instead she walked to the judge's table. "Sir, what data would you want?"
He showed her: water before and after, three samples, a simple table.
Back home she and Hemant argued behind the cowshed. "You're taking his side," he said.
"I'm taking our model's side. We didn't test it. That's true."
Hemant kicked a stone, then sighed. "Fine. You write the table. I'll collect the samples from the handpump."

qa.q: What did the judge write on Rashmi's model?
qa.a: "Idea good. Testing weak. No data."

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when she first read the mark?

qa.q: What made Rashmi's approach work with the judge and with Hemant?
qa.a: She asked the judge what data he wanted instead of arguing, and told Hemant calmly that she was on their model's side.

passage:
The Oslo youth orchestra had one rehearsal left before the spring concert. The conductor stopped the strings and said, "Lars, you rush the second bar every time."
Lars felt his jaw tighten. Sofia, sharing his music stand, whispered, "You do, a bit."
He wanted to snap that she dragged, not that he rushed. Instead he nodded. "Can we try it slower?"
They played it again. He rushed less.
At the break, Sofia said, "Sorry if I made it worse."
"You didn't," Lars said. "But next time tell me after, not while he's looking. It's easier."
She thought about it. "Fair. And you tell me when I drag."
"You drag in bar thirty," he said, and she laughed.

qa.q: Which bar did the conductor say Lars rushed?
qa.a: The second bar.

qa.q: What was Lars feeling when Sofia whispered that he did rush?
qa.a: He felt defensive and irritated; his jaw tightened and he wanted to snap back.

qa.q: What did Lars do well in handling the feedback?
qa.a: He accepted the correction, tried it again, and later calmly asked Sofia to tell him after rehearsal instead of mid-scene.

qa.q: How might Sofia have felt when Lars told her about bar thirty?
qa.a: Sofia probably felt relieved and amused that the tension had turned into fair, friendly feedback.

grounding: Shows a teen accepting criticism and settling a stand-partner conflict calmly.

At the district football academy, Coach pinned the match ratings on the board. Hemant had a five out of ten: "Lost the ball, lost your head."
Asif, the captain, read it over his shoulder. "You shouted at the ref. We got a yellow because of you."
Hemant turned. "And you never pass to me."

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when Asif blamed him for the yellow card?

Shankar stood on the metro platform in Delhi at 7 a.m. with his earphones in but nothing playing. The news on the screen showed floods in one state, a factory fire in another, a chart of rising prices.
He'd been like this for weeks. Not sad, exactly. More like the air had weight. What was the point of board exams if the planet was cooking? What was he even supposed to become in a world like this?
His friend Yash came up behind him and tugged an earphone out. "You look like you're carrying the whole city."
Shankar shrugged. "Maybe I am."
Yash didn't laugh. "Me too, some days. Want to walk from the next station? The long way?"
They walked. It didn't fix anything, but the air felt lighter.

qa.q: What did the news screen show?
qa.a: Floods in one state, a factory fire in another, a chart of rising prices.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling on the platform?
qa.a: He felt a heavy, generalised dread and frustration, as if the air had weight and nothing had a point.

qa.q: How could an adult support Shankar if this feeling keeps going?
qa.a: A parent or school counsellor could listen without dismissing his worries and help him find small things he can do and enjoy.

qa.q: What is it like for Yash when he sees Shankar that morning?
qa.a: Yash recognises the feeling because he has it too, so he responds with company rather than a joke.

grounding: Shows a teen carrying diffuse dread about the world and a friend's quiet support.

"Why are you still awake?" Anirban whispered from the top bunk.
Vinita didn't answer for a while. "Do you ever think we're too late for everything?"
"Too late for what?"
"For good jobs. For clean air. For anything to be normal. Everyone keeps saying study hard and you'll be fine. I don't believe them."
"That's a lot for midnight, didi."
"I know." She pulled the blanket up. "It's just there. All the time. Like background noise."
Anirban climbed down and sat on the edge of her bunk. "I don't know the answers. But you're not the only one. Half my class says the same."
"Really?"
"Really. Tell Maa tomorrow? She keeps asking why you're so quiet."
Vinita nodded in the dark. "Tomorrow."

qa.a: Like background noise, there all the time.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel hearing his older sister say this at midnight?

Last term I kept a list on my phone called "Why bother." I'm Vikas, and I'm a bit embarrassed by it now.
Every night I'd add something: the heat wave, the job cuts on the news, a video of melting ice. I'd lie there scrolling until two. In the morning I'd be too tired to care about school, then angry at myself for not caring.
My friend Devika noticed during a free period. "You look like someone switched you off," she said. I showed her the list. She didn't tell me to cheer up. She said, "Now write one you can do."
I wrote: plant the balcony tulsi again. Help at the Saturday clean-up. Sleep before twelve.
The dread didn't vanish. But I have two lists now, and the second one is longer.

qa.q: What was the name of the list on Vikas's phone?
qa.a: "Why bother."

qa.q: How did Devika seem to feel when she saw Vikas in the free period?
qa.a: She seemed concerned, noticing Vikas looked switched off, and caring enough to respond without brushing it off.

qa.q: What would you advise Vikas if the dread comes back strongly?
qa.a: Keep using the second list and talk to a trusted adult or school counsellor if it keeps going or worries Vikas.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had told Vikas to cheer up?
qa.a: Vikas might have felt dismissed and kept scrolling, instead of finding small things to do.

grounding: A teen recalls a spell of dread about the world and a friend's practical nudge.

Okay, Madhav, you're recording? Good. I'm Gargi, and this is about turtles.
In Class 8 we went on a beach clean-up in Chennai just to skip school. At five in the morning we saw volunteers guarding a nest with a torch. Tiny turtles scrambling for the water. I cried. In front of everyone.
Since then, I've done every night walk I'm allowed to. I made posters for our colony about switching off beach-facing lights. My mother says I talk about turtles at dinner so much the dal gets cold.
Some people think it's a phase. Maybe. But when I'm on the sand at night, I feel like the most useful version of myself.
This year I'm training juniors to do night walks too. That's my favourite part now.

qa.a: Gargi feels purposeful and deeply moved, like the most useful version of Gargi.

I'm Lakshmi, Zeenat's neighbour. She's been drawing comics since the summer holidays, and now it's taken over.
At first it was a notebook on the steps. Then she bought cheap ink pens with her pocket money. Now she's on our shared staircase every evening, with pages spread out and a torch when the bulb goes.
Last week her mother called her three times for dinner. Zeenat said, "One panel more, Ammi," three times.
She showed me a page once. It was about a girl who sells chai at a railway station. It was good. Really good.
I don't know if she'll become an artist. But when she's drawing, her whole face changes, like she's somewhere else.

First week of June: Mohit heard a debate on the radio about the new flyover cutting down old trees on his road. He didn't care much. Trees were trees.
Two weeks later: the axes started. His neighbour Salma aunty stood crying near the gulmohar that had shaded her shop for thirty years. Mohit watched, fists in pockets, and felt something shift.
By August: he had joined a citizens' group, learned the names of every tree on the road, and was spending weekends with a measuring tape and a register. His mother complained his room smelt of paper and mud.
One Sunday he spoke at a small meeting, voice trembling. Afterwards Salma aunty patted his cheek. "You care more than I did at your age," she said.

qa.q: Which tree had shaded Salma aunty's shop?
qa.a: The gulmohar, for thirty years.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel watching the axes?
qa.a: He felt upset and angry, standing with fists in his pockets as something shifted in him.

qa.q: What could help Mohit keep his passion going without burning out?
qa.a: Sharing tasks with the citizens' group and keeping time for rest and school would help him last.

qa.q: How might Salma aunty feel about Mohit's efforts?
qa.a: Salma aunty seems touched and grateful, patting his cheek and saying he cares more than she did at his age.

grounding: Tracks a teen's growing commitment to saving trees over a summer.

passage:
When the Tokyo swim club posted the relay team, Aiko's name wasn't on it. She shrugged. "I didn't want to swim relay anyway."
Nkechi, her friend from the changing rooms, raised an eyebrow. "You've been training for it since April."
"It's just swimming. Who cares."
Aiko stopped staying after practice. She scrolled her phone on the bench and said everything was boring. Her coach asked if something was wrong. "Nope. Just over it."
Two weeks later, Nkechi found her crying in the car park. "I care so much it's stupid," Aiko said. "If I act like I don't, it doesn't hurt."
Nkechi sat with her. "It hurts anyway. Might as well have company."
The next morning Aiko asked the coach what she needed to improve.

qa.q: When had Aiko been training for the relay since?
qa.a: Since April.

qa.q: Why did Aiko say it was just swimming and she was over it?
qa.a: She was hurt and embarrassed at being left off, and acting uncaring felt safer than admitting how much it mattered.

qa.q: How could a coach help a swimmer who suddenly acts bored?
qa.a: The coach could gently check in again in private and offer clear steps to improve, so caring feels safe again.

qa.q: What is it like for Nkechi to watch Aiko pretend not to care?
qa.a: Nkechi can see through it and feels concerned, which is why she stays and sits with her.

grounding: Shows a teen masking disappointment with indifference until a friend helps her face it.

The school counsellor's room smelt of new paint. Jahnavi slumped in the chair, arms crossed.
"Your class teacher says you've stopped handing in work," said Sangeeta ma'am.
"Doesn't matter."
"What doesn't?"
"Any of it. Marks. Plans. It's all whatever."
Sangeeta ma'am waited. The fan clicked. Then she asked, "When did it last matter?"
Jahnavi's jaw moved. "Before my parents said we're moving again. Third city in four years. Why try if I'm leaving?"
"So not caring keeps it from hurting."
Jahnavi shrugged, but her eyes filled.
"We can work on what's hard about moving," Sangeeta ma'am said. "And I'd like to talk with your parents too, if you agree."
Jahnavi nodded once.

qa.q: What news did Jahnavi's parents give?
qa.a: That they are moving again, the third city in four years.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling underneath saying "It's all whatever"?
qa.a: She felt hurt and sad about moving again, and not caring kept it from hurting.

qa.q: What small step did Sangeeta ma'am take, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She asked when it last mattered and offered to talk with Jahnavi's parents, getting to the real cause instead of scolding.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's parents feel if they learned about her detachment?
qa.a: They may feel worried and sorry, not having realised how hard the moves were on her.

grounding: Shows a teen using detachment to protect herself from the pain of repeated moves.

Dear Sumit,
I owe you an apology for the science exhibition.
When our model collapsed an hour before judging, you were trying to fix it and I just sat there saying "It's only an exhibition, bro, chill." You thought I didn't care. I did. That's the problem.
I had spent three weeks on the wiring. When it fell, I felt so stupid that pretending not to care was easier than admitting I was gutted. So I acted bored and left you to do everything.
I'm sorry. You deserved a partner, not a shrug.
Can we fix it together this weekend and enter the district round? I'll bring the soldering iron and actual effort this time.
Jatin
